To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the anti-HIV pyrimidines can be considered as a chemical system whose bonding mechanism is governed by the LoSMoC and BraS SMILES forms.

the anti-HIV mechanism of pyrimidine derivatives is driven by the SMILES transformation and that the LoSMoC and BraS structures are the main forms responsible for the anti-HIV potential of pyrimidines.

the LoSMoC and BraS forms of the SMILES structures of pyrimidines are the main chemical-biological intermediates involved in the anti HIV activity mechanism of pyrimidinones, pyrimidinethiones and pyrimidinecarboxylic acids, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the chemical reactivity driving biological activity of the anti-HIV pyrimidines.

the molecular mechanism of the anti-HIV action of the selected pyrimidines and with the molecular pathways leading to the biological sites of the HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT) and HIV-1 integrase (IN) as the target enzymes.

the development of a novel QSAR methodology based on the chemical reactivity principles and on the SMILES transformations of a series of uracil derivatives, which can be applied to any other series of chemical structures, in the perspective of the molecular mechanism of chemical-biological interactions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the LoSMoC is a necessary intermediate in the molecular pathway of the pyrimidine docking at the biological site and that the BraS is a necessary intermediate of the molecular pathway of pyrimidine binding at the biological site, respectively.
the LoSMoC form, as a molecular intermediate of the uracil anti-HIV activity, is a chemical reactivity-driven structure that can be considered as a chemical-biological bonding mechanism.

the anti-HIV pyrimidine bonding mechanism is driven by the chemical power and electrophilicity of the Longest SMILE Molecular Chain and Branching SMILES, respectively, and the chemical hardness of the Longest Molecular SMILES Chain and the chemical hardness and electrophilic index of the Branching SMILEs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LoSMoC form is a more reactive species than the BraS form.

chemical reactivity principles can be applied in the context of SMILES transformations to determine chemical bonding mechanisms of biological activity and to establish the main molecular pathways of a given chemical-biological interaction.
the LoSMoC form is the most reactive and the BraS form is the most stable form of a pyrimidine, and the most reactive form of a pyrindine would have the best activity as an anti-HIV drug.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the chemical reactivity descriptors are able to provide the molecular mechanism of the anti-HIV pyrimidines and to identify the main chemical bonding stages of the SMILES transformation, which can be considered as the main molecular pathways involved in the HIV inhibition.
a chemical reactivity-based approach can be successfully employed in order to establish a quantitative relationship between chemical structures and biological activity.
